subtopic: * TRANSPORT DEPARTMENT REGULATIONS, JET AIRCRAFT NOISE
* TRANSPORT DEPARTMENT REGULATIONS, JET AIRCRAFT NOISE
speechtext:
1.	What are the present regulations of the Department of Transport concerning the control of noise levels of jet aircraft?
2.	What are the methods of enforcement of these regulations?
3.	What improvements to these regulations are being considered?
[Mr. Jorgenson.)

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: * TRANSPORT DEPARTMENT REGULATIONS, JET AIRCRAFT NOISE
speechtext:
1. Section 516 of the air regulations states in part that "the pilot in command of an aircraft operating on or in the vicinity of an aerodrome should conform with any directions made by the minister relating to noise abatement".
The aforementioned "directions" are set forth as a part of the operating certificate issued in respect of each commercial air service and in notices to airmen (NOTAMS); aircraft operating on or in the vicinity of certain aerodromes are required to conform with certain laid down procedures calculated to reduce the noise level.
2.	(a) By keeping visual and radar watch on all aircraft operations and by monitoring the noise levels created by turbine powered aircraft, particularly in noise critical areas, and
(b) By continual liaison with the operators to ensure their co-operation and compliance with noise abatement directives.
An operator who does not comply with the laid down noise abatement procedures can be said to have contravened not only section 516 but also sections 813 and 814 of the air regulations. Section 813 states in part that "neglect on the part of any person to whom any licence, certificate or permit has been issued under these regulations of any precaution that may be required by the ordinary practices of the air or by the special circumstances of the case, or the contravention of these regulations or any direction of the minister thereunder is cause for suspension of such licence, certificate or permit." Section 814 states that "failure on the part of any person to whom any licence, certificate or permit has been issued under these regulations to observe or comply with the conditions of issue of such licence, certificate or permit shall be deemed to constitute a contravention of these regulations by such person".
3.	No changes to these regulations are being considered at this time; however, noise abatement requirements are under constant review by officials of the department and operating standards and procedures may be changed from time to time in the light of experience gained.

Mr. Speaker, on Thursday I told the house that my department was investigating a newspaper report from Britain concerning the drug preludin. To bring the house up to date, I should like to advise that on Friday afternoon my department received the item that apparently led to this public interest. It consists of one letter in the latest issue of the British medical journal, referring to a patient who was unfortunate enough to lose a child in 1958 and another in 1960 after having taken this drug. By that time we had

asked for reports from London and Washington, though we had no indication that either Britain or the United States felt there was cause for concern. While the United States food and drug administration is investigating the matter, it has not produced any incriminating evidence that would justify action being taken.
The Italian ministry of health has informed us that the decision to ban the drug and similar preparations pending the outcome of study it has just initiated was taken as a result of the medical journal article, and not because of any reports that these medicines have been associated with infant deformities in Italy. We are continuing to investigate this situation, and if any action should seem appropriate it will certainly be taken. In view of the drug's history in wide international use, though, I do not believe there is reason to be alarmed solely by one report of what may be a medical coincidence.
The attending doctors in the British case make it clear that they are recalling this case because of current examination of the general problem, and I am sure they would be surprised to see the weight that has been attached to their letter in some quarters. On the other side, we must remember that the drug has been on sale under prescription in Canada for six years, with no reports of such problems having arisen.

The request of the government for this supply is necessary in order to carry out certain activities of which we have received formal notice from you, Mr. Chairman, and also more particularly by the further supplementary estimates that were tabled this day. At the very beginning I draw attention to the fact that on the last occasion on which interim supply was requested we did not take advantage of the motion to discuss matters which, as I said earlier, were of particular

interest to our members. We took this decision in the interests of getting on with the business of the house. We took this decision in order to assist the public interest and the public business and in the expectation that the government would bring on, in an orderly fashion, its legislative program.
We have now been sitting in this House of Commons for over two months. When we came here in the month of September I think we had every reason to anticipate and expect that we would be dealing with at least two things which we thought were of importance. The first was the long term measures and long term program which the government had in mind, having to do with the economic position of our country, as was stated by the Prime Minister during the campaign and was stated also by government members and the Prime Minister thereafter. We also anticipated that we would be dealing with the budget.
However, the expectation we held at that time has not been realized. We are not satisfied, Mr. Chairman, that the work of the house is being properly organized and that the program of the government is being brought forward in a systematic fashion. Instead, we have been asked to deal with a series of measures which I would not dare say were unimportant; however, they certainly were not our conception of what was described by the government as matters of urgent importance.
I have here a summary of the legislation we have dealt with thus far. It includes the national health act-the Food and Drugs Act. We have still to have third reading of that measure. Had this act been referred to a committee, as was suggested from this side of the chamber, I am sure that it would have been through in no time. Certainly it would have gone through by this time. Then there were the Farm Credit Act, the Export Credits Insurance Act and the tax bills.
The three tax bills took no time whatever. What took a long time, of course-and the committee will remember this-was the general debate which was agreed upon by all parties and which was inaugurated on the first resolution. However, I should like to point out this fact to the minister and to the committee. Instead of having a general debate without a budget, if the government had brought down a budget the budget would have been through in less than the time taken on the general debate, because the rules of the house would have so prescribed. We disposed of the Income Tax Act and the Excise Tax Act, and the Estate Tax Act went through very quickly. The Customs Act, of course, did not take an undue length of time. As the

committee knows, an amendment is still pending at the present time. There are a number of other items which are now on the order paper. I think of those having to do with the Judges Act, the Department of Transport and the Freight Rates Reduction Act which, as the committee knows, expired on April 30 last. Still there has been no attempt to deal with that matter.
As I read the further supplementary estimates that were tabled by the minister today the first thing that struck me was vote No. 213a, $50 million for interim payments, related to the recommendations of the royal commission on railway problems. It is the same vote in the same amount with the same wording as vote No. 590 tabled in the house some time earlier. This is an indication that thus far the government has not yet been able to make up its mind with reference to these recommendations.
The responsibility for organizing the work of the house and the business of the house rests fully with the government. That responsibility can only be discharged by the government; consequently it must accept the chief responsibility for the lack of legislative output.
We have examined our participation in most of the debates that have been held thus far during this session. I believe we can demonstrate that we have not taken nearly as much time in proportion to our numbers as the other opposition groups or the government members. We wish to urge upon the government the necessity of following a more certain and systematic course in arranging and forecasting the business of the house. I should like to refer here to a few examples.
The leader of the house has from time to time called a number of items. He has called items which the house has never dealt with. He has called items which were dealt with on one day and then held up for a period of days or even weeks; then we would come back to them later. The resolution, which was first brought before the house on Thursday, October 18 and Friday, October 19, took only a very short time, I believe two and a half hours of discussion on the latter day. Mr. Chairman, the Liberals have taken the time of the house in trying to question certain experts, certain advisers, certain personalities, or in trying to obtain documents so as to see, as much as they possibly could, whether the Conservative government, and more especially the Prime Minister, had misled the people before the last election by keeping secret the coming crisis and its effects, such as our decreased foreign exchange reserves.
As far as we are concerned, we knew very well what was coming: we did not have to question anyone. We knew all about it, and we are satisfied that the government knew all about it, just as they knew about the austerity program they would have to bring about. It is a fact that the steps that were taken a few days following the election should normally have been taken several months before that, for we could tell that the crisis was constantly worsening. We were foreseeing the crisis which we would have to face and which would bring about austerity, credit restrictions, tariff surcharges, the freezing of the salaries of civil servants, etc. We were aware of all that. Even though the

Prime Minister refuses to admit it, it is a fact that, for the last several years, Canada was heading towards this crisis that we are now facing.
Mr. Chairman, we are now being asked to approve interim supply. We are ready to agree to the proposal which the hon. member for Laurier made a moment ago, concerning the legislation to be brought down between now and the Christmas recess. However, I should like to mention that we have to consider expenditures which have not yet been dealt with nor accepted. The budget itself was brought down several months ago-eight months I think-and today a supplementary budget is submitted to us. Now, we have not considered nor accepted those budget estimates. In fact, we are asked today to vote amounts of money, including the 1962-63 supplementary budget, that have been spent, namely, for instance, as indicated on page 8 of supplementary estimates, in the last line:
(Text):
Expenses of the royal commission on banking and finance, $166,630.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, that amount has been appropriated for the royal commission on banking and finance. We had asked that experts, advisers and representatives of our party be present at the examination of Messrs. Coyne and Towers.
The money was spent and we did not have our say in the matter. Those expenditures were made without anyone taking the least notice of our suggestions that representatives of the four parties be allowed to attend the sittings of that commission. Therefore, the government has spent the money, and there is almost nothing left of those estimates submitted today.
I feel that this is rather abnormal, but in an attempt to hasten the introduction of important measures that might be brought before the house, the members of our party will refrain from discussing any further this interim supply introduced today.
(Text):

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is quite usual when a government asks for interim supply to request that it be granted with a minimum amount of debate. It also happens fairly often that the house agrees to such a request. We are witnessing that request and that kind of response in general terms again today. I am sure that we understand the situation in which we find ourselves, and I am sure too that we are ready to be co-operative.
Interim Supply
However, I believe we do have to take a moment to look at the way in which we are, in effect, painting ourselves into a corner. By the time the bill based on this interim supply resolution has been passed we will have voted nine twelfths of all the money in the main and supplementary estimates for the 1962-63 fiscal year. In some cases we will have voted ten twelfths and in some cases eleven twelfths. Yet, Mr. Chairman, at this point we have not passed a single item of the main or supplementary estimates. In fact, so far as this parliament is concerned we have had discussion on only one of them, namely the first item in the Department of Agriculture.
Now, where are we going? The Minister of Finance says that within a few days he will bring down another request for interim supply for another 30 days. By that point we will have voted ten twelfths of everything and eleven twelfths of many items. If this trend continues, before we know it we will be approaching the end of the 1962-63 fiscal year. I can see a point coming when the minister will say, "Now we are almost at the end of the year. This year is gone, so what does it matter? Let us look at next year and pass these items expeditiously." The committee will be given several hundred items of the main and supplementary estimates and will be asked to put them through. If we want to talk on any which may be important there will be members of the government or of the Liberal or Social Credit parties who will say we will be wasting time.
We feel we should give very serious consideration to the kind of position that parliament is being put in by this shoe-horning method under which the government is getting its money for this fiscal year.
I think the hon. member for Laurier is perfectly justified in saying that a similar situation has developed with respect to legislation. Debate has started on a number of items on the order paper, but frequently when a debate waxes warm or when it looks like there might be a crucial vote, the debate is adjourned. Therefore we have quite a mixture of estimates that have not been dealt with and important items of legislation which have not been put through, at a time when we are coming to the end of the calendar and fiscal year, the end of the time during which this session of parliament should deal with its business.
I believe something along the line suggested by the hon. member for Laurier should be considered by the government, namely that there should be some kind of conference at the top level of all four parties in the house to consider where we are going with respect to the estimates for this fiscal year and with

Interim Supply
respect to this session's business. It is obvious that the government has not been able to give the kind of leadership parliament needs in order to get measures passed through the house, and I suggest that it is time the government called together representatives of all the other parties to try to plan the business of this session with respect to both estimates and legislation.
I can assure the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister that if any effort is made along that line we shall do our best to cooperate in getting important measures through the house. However, I must say that although we are quite firm in our offer to co-operate, this does not take away the responsibility that rests upon us to draw to the attention of the government, the house and the country those things which we think the government is doing that are wrong.
I know my hon. friends across the way, judging by remarks made by the hon. member for Red Deer the other day, think it is a waste of time to indulge in procedural debates on some of these things, but on my desk right now there is an answer to some questions that appeared on today's order paper which disposes of that contention. My question No. 900 read as follows:
1.	From June 24, 1962, to October 31, 1962, how many remissions of customs duties were made under the provisions oi section 2 of the Surcharge on Imports Order, P.C. 1962-902, as based on section 22 of the Financial Administration Act?
2.	How many of these remissions were for amounts of $1,000 or more?
3.	To whom was each remission of $1,000 or more made, and what was the amount in each case?
I asked that question because this sort of thing has been questioned in the house and because I wanted to be sure that the provisions of the act were being carried out. The Minister of Finance, when he was questioned about this the other day by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River said, as recorded on page 1788 of Hansard for November 19:
All I can say in reply to that question is that I am no longer minister of national revenue, but I am quite certain I do not have to assure the committee that the provisions of the Financial Administration Act are being complied with by the Department of National Revenue.
What is the provision of the Financial Administration Act on which my question was based? It is section 22, subsection 8 which reads as follows:
A statement of each remission of one thousand dollars or more granted under this section shall be reported to the House of Commons in the Public Accounts.
Mr. Chairman, that is the reason I worded my question as I did. I did not ask for lower amounts. I asked only for those of $1,000 or more because that is what the act requires

and because the Minister of Finance said the other day that the committee could be assured that the Department of National Revenue was complying with the provisions of the Financial Administration Act.
This is the answer I got today and which will appear in today's Hansard:
The information requested is not available as detailed statistics are not maintained pertaining to the application of the surcharge on imports order.
That is a clear breach of the law.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: It is just as clear a breach of the law as we had on other occasions in the past.
The Auditor General will comment on that.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I must read the whole answer.
The next sentence presents an excuse, but I submit that an excuse is not satisfactory when the law is being broken. The rest of the answer reads as follows:
To present a complete answer would entail a careful examination of approximately 2,205,235 import entries passed at 276 ports of entry in Canada.
I grant that it is a tall order to keep track of all these things, but, Mr. Chairman, the law is the law. This is the place where we make laws. This is the place where we talk about the rule of law, and this is the place where we say the law must be kept. This is the place where, a few days ago, the Minister of Finance said he could give us the assurance that the Department of National Revenue was complying with the provisions of the Financial Administration Act.
And nobody should question the deputy attorney general.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Oh, we must not do things like that, but this is a provision of the act. It is crystal clear; and the surcharge on imports order, at least half of it, is based on section 22 of the Financial Administration Act. We were assured the other day that the law was being complied with, but when I asked for this kind of information I was told:
The information requested is not available as detailed statistics are not maintained pertaining to the application of the surcharge on imports order.
In other words, this government has not only seen fit to pass an order in council, which in my view has no validity at all, but having passed it, it now refuses to carry out the provisions of the section in the Financial Administration Act under which it claims it had the right to pass that surcharge order.
Shocking.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I hope the word "shocking" is on Hansard. As a matter of fact I wish Hansard could record the stillness there was in the house a moment ago when I first read that answer. No matter what our views might be about the government in power today, we did not think this of the government. We did not think that having passed an order in council based on a section in a statute of parliament it would then not only refuse to carry out that instruction but would have the gall to say so without a moment's hesitation in answer to a question on the order paper.
I put my question on the order paper only a few days ago and I was surprised that the answer was given today. I thought the question would have to stand for a few days to enable the department to get the information, but this was not the case. The government in effect stated it did not intend to carry out the provisions of the statute. However, we do now know how many import entries there were. There have been 2,205,235 during the period under review, but the government has not kept statistics for the purpose of complying with the provision in the statute on the basis of which the order in council was passed.
I say to my hon. friend from Red Deer, because I was chilled the other day about the things he said; that we were taking up too much time in discussing these things-
Vital constitutional matters.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
We are talking about the same thing. We are talking about getting to the bottom of the legislation on which the imports surcharge order was passed. We are talking about whether it was brought in with proper validity, and now we know that the government is not complying with the statutory provision under which it claims the right to pass that order in council. This makes it more necessary to sit down with the government to discuss how to get along with the business of the house, but I say to the government that if we do sit down together we will want some pretty frank answers to questions about this kind of thing.
This is not leadership in a democracy; this is not leadership of the House of Commons. It is not getting on with the business of the country to treat parliament in this way. This is why we have been painted into a corner, to use a phrase I used a few moments ago, in terms of the estimates of this house, in terms of the legislation before us, and other such matters. It is because there does not seem to have been a facing up to what is required, under the rule of law, with respect to the leadership of parliament at this time, that I urge, before parliament gets into
Interim Supply
greater disrepute because of this kind of thing, that there should be a more realistic approach to what is necessary in order tc put this session on the rails.
There are one or two more things I want to say, but since we are in committee of supply and we can speak more than once there will be an opportunity of raising these other matters later. I want to urge, now, that this House of Commons should realize where we are in terms of the grant of money we are being asked to vote. Before we vote we should realize where we are in terms of the legislation of this session-a session which is fast moving on-and in terms of how the government is treating a matter as important as a provision of one of the statutes of parliament itself.

I do not intend to deal with the particular matter which was raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. That will be dealt with by the Minister of Finance. I will only say that in so far as the legality of what has been done in putting into effect the surcharges is concerned, I would prefer the opinion of the law officers of the crown to the view of the hon. gentleman on the subject. It is perfectly clear to us that we must accept this legal opinion that what was done was done within the powers granted by parliament to the executive; and in the discharge of those powers we acted as we did.
I rise for the purpose of discussing in general a charge which I think has become perennial and continual. As far back as I can read, and on every occasion for the past 25 years or more, whenever a vote has been asked of parliament in this way the argument has been advanced that there is something wrong, that there had not been on the part of the government that leadership which would assure the proper and effectual operation of parliament. I intend, first, to deal with what has taken place.
Governments propose, and oppositions dispose. There is only one way in which a government can carry through its legislative program if an opposition has its eye on certain objectives desirable for the opposition but not desirable from the point of view of an effectual operation of parliament, and that is through the medium of closure. That is something to which, on the basis of the experience of the past, this government does not intend to resort. I wish to make that very clear. I listened with interest to the statement made by the hon. member for Laurier-his offer of co-operation. I welcome that offer of cooperation now, although I point out that for

Interim Supply
the past 41 days there has been nothing indicative of an attitude of co-operation on the part of the opposition.
That statement is not true.

The hon. gentlemen must feel the pangs of conscience or they would not be interrupting. They recognize their guilt. Recognizing that guilt, they start making observations from a seated position which often, in the case of the hon. member, is representative of the most intelligent things he does.
I go back. I intend to review what has happened. The longer I see parliament in operation, the more I hold the view that reforms are necessary in order to assure a greater acceleration of its business. That has been so throughout the years. Let us examine the change of rules which we brought about. Parliament sits from 2.30 p.m. until ten o'clock at night. Of this time, from 2.30 p.m. to 5 p.m. is spent on government business and from 5 p.m. to 6 p.m. on private members' resolutions. From 8 p.m. to 10 p.m. the house again considers government business. In the result, we sit five and a half hours a day, four and a half of them on government business and one on private members' resolutions.
I am not criticizing private members' resolutions, for out of the discussion of those resolutions legislative enactments are often ultimately introduced. They educate; they place before the people viewpoints which otherwise might not receive attention. But the fact remains that actually, in the operation of government, with the exception of the debate on the address, the total length of time we sit is from 2.30 p.m. to 5 p.m., that is, two and a half hours, and from 8 p.m. to 10 p.m., or a total of four and a half hours a day.
I recognize the difficulties for private members in this regard, and also for ministers, but I believe we may well have to consider an extension of the hours of sitting of parliament. When one considers that in a five day week we sit some 30 hours-I have not totalled it up-a reform in this direction would, it seems to me, be beneficial and helpful.
All of us have had this experience: we sit short hours when there is work to be done and then, when we come toward the end of a session, we expand and expand those hours of sitting to an extent which denies members-and I am speaking of the private members-the opportunity to fully consider the various measures which come before the house.
It is all very well to say that there is a failure on the part of the government to give leadership. I am going to refer to the orders

of the day. Legislation is ready; we want to proceed. Let us just examine an ordinary day. More and more, with the passing years, longer and longer periods of time are being taken up by questions on the orders of the day. What about the British parliament? It does not operate on that basis at all. It sits longer hours. In addition, questions are not asked before orders of the day without notice. The questions which are asked must appear on the order paper and then there can be supplementary questions. When I first came to this house-and the hon. member for Essex East, the hon. member for Laurier as well as the leader of the New Democratic party were here in those years-one or two questions might be asked on the orders of the day, and that was the limit. But as time has gone on, it has expanded. We finally arrive at the point when, by 1945, if we had three questions on one day we thought we were par on this course.
And so it has expanded to the point where today we spend 45 minutes, 50 minutes, and even 60 minutes on questions. I like questions which are penetrating. They may hurt my personal sensitivities at the moment, or those of the government; but if you examine the questions asked on an average day-and I criticize no one member-there is not one in a carload which would embarrass anybody. This is being developed more and more. I am not here to mention what his honour Mr. Speaker has done in order to keep these questions within the rules of parliament, but if we set an average sessional year of 140 days, with an hour a day for questions, that is 140 hours spent on questions. If we sat 35 hours a week instead of 30, there you have four weeks of questions; four weeks of the sittings of this house spent on orders of the day. I am not here speaking of questions on the order paper. No wonder there has been an expansion in the time of sittings. Furthermore, a government, and parliament itself, is in the grip of rules which deny any real action being taken in the early days of a session.
Now let me deal with the 41 days on which we have already sat. The speech from the throne took 10 days. That is the regular period. There is nothing we can do about that excepting agree not to talk and to bring on the vote at an early date. Ways and means took nine days. A supply motion took two days. There are 21 days in which no legislative action could be taken.
What about legislative action? Seventeen days have been spent on legislative action. Three days were spent on the Export Credits Insurance Act. No amount of leadership on the part of the government can get legislation

through earlier. Hon. members want to express themselves and they should have that opportunity. There is only one control within the rules over the length of time an hon. member speaks, and that is his own conscience in determining how much shorter a period he can speak and still bring the message and the viewpoint he wishes to put before parliament. The Farm Credit Act took six days. I am not placing the blame on anybody in that regard because everyone wanted the Farm Credit Act. Everyone wants action; and yet we spent six full days on discussing that matter. The Food and Drugs Act, which concerns the Department of National Health and Welfare, is one that naturally mobilizes the thinking of members, their fears and desires to do what they can to help. That took two days. The Combines Investigation Act has taken one day. The resolution on industrial change and manpower adjustment has taken one day. Budget bills took four days. There you have 17 days on those matters.
Hon. members say, why do we not bring the legislation forward? It is ready; it is drawn. But we find ourselves in a position where there are only so many hours in a day, and we have reduced those hours to such a minimum that we are not effectively carrying out our responsibilities. There is no reason in the world why we should not sit longer hours. I know it might be difficult for some hon. members who live close to Ottawa and in the adjoining two central provinces, but the rest of the hon. members are here all the time. They cannot get home when they want to at any time. So I think the suggestion of the hon. member is one which deserves consideration. By agreement we could extend the period of sittings. I do not think there would be any strong opposition to action in that regard, particularly between now and the Christmas holiday.
There used to be a time, not so very long ago, when some hon. gentlemen were predicting that parliament would be out in a week, or out in two weeks. One hon. gentleman, who is a profound student of constitutional development, said that in his opinion we would be out within 30 days, and he said: "I'll bet my shirt on it." Well, he still has his shirt and we still have parliament. But we do not hear so much about those predictions any more; so we can get away from infighting on the question of the dissolution of the house and down to infighting on the question of legislation, and let us get this legislative program before parliament.
What about the rest? The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said that we had not got down yet to any of the estimates. All we
Interim Supply
have discussed is agriculture, for a period of two days. Then there was one day, Wednesday, October 17, when we did not do any business at all, when arguments went back and forth on an appeal from the Speaker's ruling.
There is the record on this forty second day of the session. The legislation is available. We are ready to present it. If hon. members do not think so, just let them pass this supply, and pass these bills one after the other, and they will get them fast. That is all I ask.
Oh, oh.

It is all right to say: "We do not know about that". Just place us in the position of not having the legislation available. But it is here; it is ready.
Now let me point out that there are 29 pieces of legislation ready. I am not one of those who argues that there should be any interference with the right of hon. members to express themselves, but I do agree with the hon. member that if the house leaders of the parties could get together and apportion the time, it would be a most effective and welcome expedient in order to achieve a high degree of efficiency in parliament. They do it in the United Kingdom, but we have never been able to do it here. It becomes more difficult-this is not a matter of criticism- when there is a multiplicity of parties. That means a multiplicity of viewpoints, and it becomes more difficult to achieve. But if out of this discussion today we can bring about agreement to apportion the days between now and the Christmas adjournment, we will have made a tremendous advance in parliamentary reform of our own volition.
I would add to what the hon. gentleman said about an agreement, providing the party leaders could be brought to agree that, as we do not have very long between now and the Christmas adjournment, we sit in the mornings. There is no reason in the world why we should not. Again, on Wednesdays we could sit in the evenings. We could increase the time of sittings by eight or ten hours a week. No one would be harmed and all of us would have made that little sacrifice which always brings warmth to the hearts of those who participate by agreement.
Mention has been made of the long term plan. If we get this legislation through we will get the long term plans in addition to what is already before us in connection with those budget items which will be beneficial.
I am asked by the hon. gentleman what we can proceed with. Mention was made of redistribution; it should have been a year ago. I will not get into an argument on that.

Interim Supply
I pointed out last April when the bill was before the house that it cannot be proceeded with until after the census is completed, and the census was not completed until the month of May, as I now recollect it. We have the legislation ready. That is something that should be done. We are going to place before you the names of those who we believe would constitute a commission on redistribution which will be acceptable to hon. members in all parts of the house and will put an end to the operations on constituencies without anaesthetic which for so long has characterized redistribution in this country.
As far as major bills are concerned, let us proceed at once to deal with item No. 12. The reason for any delay in bringing ahead the redistribution measure was simply the fact that we wanted to get some of these economic measures passed by the house. There is on the order paper item No. 12, an act respecting industrial change and manpower adjustment; item No. 19, to introduce a measure to amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act; and item No. 20, to provide for the payment of certain provincial taxes and fees by crown corporations. If it is passed, it will be retroactive to April 1 and will meet a demand we have had through the years for a greater share of taxation being levied as against crown corporations, and also the removal of certain taxes which in the past have rested on provincial governments. Then there are the measures now before the house.
Mention has been made of long term plans. The national economic development board is a major one in the field of operations in this connection. In addition to that, there is the Atlantic development board. These are two measures which I would hope would receive immediate attention and be passed by parliament. These are measures which will cover the future or the economic development of the future while also having regard to the present. Then there is the item on the national productivity council and the amendments in connection therewith. When these measures have received attention as well as those that are to have third reading, namely items Nos. 1 and 2, we shall have further measures to place before you.
When I invite you to extend the hours of sitting, I do so with the recognition that we have the legislation available. In addition to that, of course, there will be other measures of a strictly economic and fiscal nature which will have to await the bringing in of the budget which I hope, as was stated some time earlier by the Minister of Finance, would be introduced at an earlier date than has ordinarily been the case. In other words, what we have been doing is placing before

you those things which can be done now, those subjects which are necessary now. They include some of our long term measures. In addition to those, we have measures to place before the house which we believe will be of great importance in meeting our problems, and in particular in the long run our payments difficulties which have been with us for years.
I wish to say to the hon. member for Laurier that I hope he and the other house leaders of the various parties will get together and that, in unanimity and that spirit of co-operation he advocated in his opening remarks, we do what we can to clear the order paper between now and the Christmas adjournment. Then, of course, the question will arise as to how long that adjournment should be. That is a matter which might also be given consideration.
I do not think there is anything more I wish say. I think we should set up the committee on procedure again and see whether they cannot make further changes. Some benefits have resulted from those meetings in the past several years. Further meetings are necessary. I do not say; imitate the British system. However, I say that, on the basis of their experience which extends over generations, we could learn a great deal as to determining the time for debate for these various subjects. If the hon. gentleman's suggestion today is accepted, I am sure that we will make large steps forward in clearing this order paper. We have available many other matters which can and will go on the order paper. Let us determine now that, as far as the order paper is concerned, we will clear it within a week.
Oh, oh.

That will require sacrifice on the part of some who might desire to speak on the subjects. I will do my part to see that members supporting the government will co-operate in this regard. I am sure the hon. member for Red Deer will do the same as well as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam.
Oh, oh.

I really do not see that there was any reason for cynical laughter at that statement. Today we have agreed that we have a problem. That problem is the problem of parliament. It is easy enough to say that the government is responsible, that it must organize the business. How can you organize something when those in other parts of the house prefer a degree of disorganization?
Oh, oh.

They do not intend that, I am sure, but that is the result. With regard to these questions, let us get together and determine a time. I shall be most happy to have the fullest co-operation on the part of the government and, on the rules as they are, we will make parliament as efficient as they permit us to make it. In addition to that, in the longer range we will bring about changes in the organization of parliament or changes in the rules. It is always a difficult thing because some, in the interest of expediency or for other reasons, would prevent members from speaking. That is a danger against which we must guard.
Having in mind the assurance that our purpose is not that but rather to get the legislation through, I shall be most happy to join with hon. members in all parts of the house to get the order paper cleared away. We will give you much more to do. It will also enable us to bring in the further matters of legislation which are necessary. I have not taken the view that it is other parties which are responsible. The rules are there. On the other hand, I resist any suggestion of failure on the part of the government to bring the legislation before the house. It is there; it is on the order paper.
As far as questions are concerned, it is not for me to suggest but I think that the number of these questions could be greatly reduced; and if we were also to have a self-denying ordinance that, under ordinary circumstances, we would not go over half an hour on questions before orders of the day we would save 15 full days in an ordinary session without, as I see it, losing any ground that might be gained through questions or in any way interfering with the rights of the opposition.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as a rule when matters of this kind are under discussion it is the leader of the house who rises to put forward the position of the government. I am delighted that the Prime Minister, feeling that he was not only in an embarrassing position himself but that the government was also-
Neither.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
-should rise to his feet and deal with the proposal that has been put forward. I am grateful to the Prime Minister for having accepted the proposal conditionally, and having regard to what I shall say in a moment perhaps we can give some consideration to the matters that were raised. But there is no doubt, no matter what the Prime Minister says or what embellishments he places on what he has said, that there is one
Interim Supply
responsibility and one responsibility alone for the conduct of the house and that lies on the other side of the house.
Thus far we have not had order and discipline in the proposals that are ordinarily put before the house. The Prime Minister said when he rose that it was a perennial argument that parliament was not operating properly. In the years that I have been here I have raised it twice. I have no doubt it was raised before but I do not think it is perennial as the Prime Minister says it is. Be that as it may, there is no doubt that we on this side of the house had every reason to expect that within the first two months at least we would be dealing with other legislation than that do which the Prime Minister has referred. We expected, as I said earlier, that we would surely have been dealing with the budget and with long term proposals; but in the list that the Prime Minister has put before us today I can see, with but one exception, nothing of a long term nature.
The Prime Minister says that the government proposes and the opposition disposes. That depends on the kind of legislation submitted by the government and it depends upon the manner in which it is submitted. I am not going to lay any blame on any colleague of mine who sits on the other side of the house, but when you have a piece of legislation that is called on Monday night or on Friday and discussed for an hour or two and then put over for a week or ten days and brought back again, how can that be considered as demonstrating order and discipline in the house?
We also have another piece of legislation -I refer to the tariff measure-to which an amendment has been moved, and it has been put off and not called for almost ten days. How can that be considered as demonstrating order and discipline? subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT REQUIRING DISCLOSURE OF CAMPAIGN FUND CONTRIBUTIONS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, consideration be given to the advisability of introducing a measure providing (a) that specified expenditures in respect of television, radio, travel within his constituency, the printing and mailing of some literature about himself and his or his party's program incurred by or on behalf of a candidate representing a federal party in a federal election be paid out of the general revenues of Canada: (b) that any additional expenditures by a candidate or by any person or organization on his behalf be limited to a specified amount calculated on the basis of voting population; and (c) that every candidate, constituency organization or federal party and any person or organization acting for or on behalf of any one or all of them shall make full and accurate disclosure of all moneys received and of all expenditures incurred by them in respect of a federal election.
He said: When the discussion began this afternoon with regard to the business of the house I feared that by the time my resolution was called at five o'clock I might feel guilty about interrupting the work of parliament.

Canada Elections Act
However, in view of what has happened this afternoon I believe the resolution I am about to discuss is perhaps the first concrete piece of work which has been placed before the house today. I hope that in consonance with the appeal made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and other members of the house this resolution can be expeditiously adopted.
I wish to say, first of all, that neither my party nor I claim that the suggestions in the resolution before us are by any means the last word on the subject. We appreciate fully that these matters ought to be carefully studied, that every aspect of them will have to be considered by a committee of the house and by other agencies which the house may decide to consult. Nevertheless, we urge that action on this question ought no longer to be delayed and that the subject is one which should be considered as soon as possible.
This resolution is divided roughly into three parts. There is, first of all, a proposal which is new as far as this house is concerned, involving the payment of certain election expenses out of general revenue. Second, there is a limitation imposed on election expenses and, third, there are proposals regarding full and accurate disclosure both of income and expenditure during an election.
I want first to set down a few of the principles which in my view underlie the proposals before the house. They are based on the belief which, I am sure, every hon. member shares, that the democratic system ought not to depend on wealth, that it should be possible in a society such as ours for every democratic idea to be heard, and to be heard as fully as every other democratic idea; that the decision by a citizen whether or not to be a candidate ought not to be governed by the extent of his means, whether his own financial means or those of his party or his friends. I believe we would agree that the proper working of a democracy ought to be entirely independent of the wealth of a person, or of a group of persons, or of any political party in this country. I submit that the only way in which our system can be successful and in which it can work with integrity and honesty is when this limitation of financial economic means is removed as far as it is possible to do so.
It is obvious-and I say this without pointing a finger at any hon. member or any party -that the need nowadays for inordinately large expenditures in am election necessarily opens temptation to trading intellectual freedom and moral integrity for financial assistance. This is a temptation which ought to be removed in order that individuals and parties may act without any debt, direct or indirect, 
to any person or organization of whatever type for the financial assistance which they or their party have received. Furthermore, when the money which a candidate or a party use comes from sources which are not disclosed and is expended in ways which are not made public, the temptation to which I have just referred is compounded.
The only way, in my submission, in which parties can act in a genuinely democratic manner in a country such as ours, is by so arranging their affairs that every Canadian who wishes to do so may know precisely where the funds of a candidate or of a party come from, and precisely where that money is spent. In that event, not only can he be told by partisans that people and parties are carrying out their duties independently and with devotion to principle, but he could also see from the actual record that this was a fact. The history of Canadian politics is full of facts produced before parliament by committees and by research people, showing that parties in Canada have received large sums of money from organizations in this country. It is impossible for the average Canadian, no matter how well meaning he may be, to escape at least the question whether a party or person, being the recipient of a large contribution from an organization, was in any way bound by some promise to that organization. Furthermore, whether we intend it or not, we often are morally affected.
We ought always to remember that we are human and that the associations which we make from the acts in which we indulge and the things we do, the environment in which we live and the way in which we conduct our political affairs, are bound to have an influence on our minds, our conscience, and our principles. It is, I think, an exaggeration of the extent of human self-control to suggest that if one is, in fact, the recipient of a large contribution from some source he will not subconsciously, if not consciously, feel obligated to that source for the contribution. It would be entirely false to a realistic consideration of the human behaviour not to admit that such a situation is bound to produce in us, and in our reactions, something that may be undesirable for the democratic system.
To put it very simply, it is impossible for a political party or for a candidate to take a large contribution from one source, particularly if that source is a corporate organization, or any other organization, without feeling, subconsciously or otherwise, under an obligation to that source and without adopting principles, possibly without realizing it, to the benefit of the source from which the contribution came.
I am doing my best to place this subject before hon. members on as non-controversial

and non-partisan a plane as I know how. That may not result in a lively debate where interruptions and catcalls take place, but I hope it will succeed in provoking a debate which is concerned with the basis of the resolution now before us. For this reason I say it does not matter what I, together with other hon. members, may think of the other parties in this house to which we do not belong, nor does it matter what we know of investigations which have taken place in the past and the results of those investigations. I am urging hon. members to acknowledge the inescapable fact that we must limit expenditures in elections so as to remove the economic barrier to democratic behaviour. We must, above all, disclose the source of the funds so as to remove the temptation of being morally and mentally obliged to those persons or organizations from whom or through which the funds came.
Another base for the resolution I have the honour to place before the house is my conviction that there is a collective responsibility to see that elections are properly conducted: that all means are taken to remove temptation from those in political office and in positions of trust toward the people of Canada; that the evils to which I have briefly referred are, as far as human beings can do so, removed. The entire society has that responsibility. In my submission it is not enough to say that the parties ought to behave; that the individual candidate or members of parliament have a responsibility. I believe it is necessary for society as a whole, and therefore for parliament, to recognize our collective responsibility to make sure that the objectives I have indicated are attained.
I submit that in the latter years in particular, when means of propaganda have multiplied, when radio and television have been added to newspaper and meeting, when, as a matter of fact, meetings are no longer fashionable, the actual exchange of ideas among spokesmen is becoming less and less common during elections. Most of us are given the chance, if we have the money, and also through time allotted by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation without payment, merely to declare our own program and our own position without either the citizen or the opposing candidate having much opportunity to consult us or to heckle us or to question us. The assemblee contradictoire is infrequent in Quebec, and in the rest of the country it is even more infrequent.
I have noticed, as I am sure have other hon. members, that as far as the average citizen is concerned he quickly gets a surfeit of propaganda beamed and thrown at him, in which he is practically drowned. I have
Canada Elections Act
the impression as I go about during election times, that by the time election day arrives, the citizen's interest has actually been dulled, rather than sharpened, by the amount of propaganda in the newspapers, on the radio and television. In other words, I am suggesting that nowadays you can have an effective election campaign, perhaps a much more effective election campaign, through limitation of expenditure rather than through leaving expenditure unlimited, as does our present legislation. I Submit that it may well be the case-in fact I am convinced it is the case- that the average Canadian will have a much sharper interest and will know a great deal more what it is the parties are talking to him about if he listens to much less of the guff-and I am as responsible for it as any other hon. member; I claim no innocence on that score-to which he now listens, and if he has to read less of the material thrown at him, often indiscriminately.
These are the reasons why, in my opinion, the propositions in the resolution now before the house are exceedingly necessary, indeed urgent, and ought to be given the most careful consideration by parliament, and action taken on them as soon as possible after adequate study.
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words in the five minutes or so left to me about each of the propositions now before the house, and I want to deal with them in the reverse order to which they appear in the resolution. As far as disclosure of sources of funds is concerned, I point out that our present legislation requires the disclosure only of the sources of funds by the candidate and not by the party. It is frequently, if not in almost all cases, the habit of all of us in this house merely to say that we have received the funds from our local constituency organization. Mr. Speaker, I submit that that is not disclosure at all; that you must have legislation which requires the party, and the organization for which a candidate stands if he does not stand for a recognized party in the country, to declare the funds contributed to it as well as to him, if you are to have real disclosure of the source of the funds spent in an election. Furthermore, the provisions of our present legislation are inadequate in a number of other directions. I submit that it is more than time for this parliament to tighten up the sections of our elections act dealing with the disclosure of the source and expenditure of funds, for the reasons I have already indicated.
The limitation on expenditures is more and more accepted in the democratic world. In Britain the first limitation on expenditures was imposed in 1883. Ever since then these

Canada Elections Act
limits have been tightened up. As recently as 1948 the limits on the amount that a candidate can spend were made still more stringent in that country. In Quebec recently, the government there proposed legislation to the same effect although it has not yet been adopted and become part of the statute book of that province. That legislation proposes an expenditure by candidate and party combined of about 75 cents per voter, although there is a difference made between city and country. Seventy five cents per voter in Canada would mean over $5 million to a party and its candidates which is hardly a limitation at all, unless, of course, the Liberal party has such large sources of funds that $5 million or $6 million represents a limitation on expenditure for it. It does not represent that to my party. The limitation which ought to be placed on expenditure, without my attempting to give any figures, is one which would bring the expenditure within the reach of every citizen in Canada who has the confidence of his fellow citizens to be a candidate for election to this parliament. That is the limitation which should be reached, and only then will we have a limit which makes sense.
Finally, a word about payment out of the treasury for certain expenditures. I appreciate that that is something new in Canada, and the proposed legislation in the province of Quebec to which I referred suggests that the treasury repay 15 cents out of the 75 cents or 80 cents, as the case may be, expended per voter. As far as I know that is the first attempt in Canada to suggest payment out of the public funds.
I hasten to urge hon. members not to be too much disturbed by that suggestion, as if it were something terribly esoteric. I remind them, if they do not remember, that in Britain the candidates for a long time paid the returning officers' expenses, and it was not until 1918 that that requirement was removed and the returning officers' expenses were paid out of the public treasury. In our country, we accepted the notion that the public treasury pay for that kind of expense ever since Canada has been a nation. After all, what is now suggested is merely an extension of the same principle. May I hasten to add that I am fully aware of the necessity carefully to limit the items for which money from the public treasury could be made available, of the necessity carefully to limit the amounts and to confine them- it I may have one second I will finish my sentence, Mr. Speaker-within limits which the people of Canada will understand and approve. If that is done and the limitation

I have suggested adopted, I am confident that we shall have a much healthier democracy than we have now.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) upon his motion. I do not wish to get into an argument at this stage of the debate with my good friend from York South. However, the members of the unions in Bow River suggest that this is correct. Maybe they misunderstand what the deduction is for. Nevertheless there appears to be some form of deduction more or less made for the support of the New Democratic party.
The suggestion before the house is that a specified amount should be spent by a candidate in the election in reference to television, radio and travel and that this amount is to be deducted from the general revenues of Canada. Then I take it that the second suggestion is that in any additional expenditure

there must be a specified amount calculated on the basis of the voting population. Then I understand that the third suggestion is that there must be a control as to how much is spent and of course that a proper form be filed in that regard.
It is rather interesting, of course, to note that, no matter how you dish this argument out, the expenses for elections have been increasing over the years. For example, I have obtained some figures with regard to the matter. First, I will deal with the country itself. These figures refer to the cost of elections. In 1949 the country spent $4,328,118. In 1953 it spent $5,380,436. In 1957 the figure had jumped to $7,500,000. In 1958 it jumped to $9,800,000. When all the expenses are added in for the last election in 1962, it cost the country $10,250,000, and this figure is not yet complete.
I would ask hon. members to keep those figures in mind. The last election cost us at least $10,500,000 more or less. The reason I have outlined these figures is in order to point out that in 1949, it would have cost the country then, if they paid all expenses, approximately $6 million. In 1953 it would have cost the country about $8 
million. In 1957 it would have cost the country about $11 million; and in 1958 it would have cost the country approximately $13 million. With regard to the question of specified expenditures being paid out of the general revenues of Canada, I suggest we must realize that elections are now costing a lot of money, particularly the last three elections which in some instances have resulted in minority groups as in 1957 and 1962, and in addition we do not know what is before us at the present time. On that basis I say that I am opposed to such a large amount of money being paid out of the general revenues of Canada when the money has to be provided by the taxpayers of this country. That is the first point I wish to make.
The second point I wish to make, as I said at the beginning, is that every person is different and reacts differently to circumstances. May I also suggest that in this great country each of our 265 constituencies is different. What it might cost one candidate or a number of candidates in one constituency to conduct an election campaign might be an inadequate amount in another constituency and too much in another.
By way of example I want to refer to my own constituency of Bow River. Those few members of the house who have not visited the province of Alberta may be unfamiliar with the fact that in that constituency alone there are five distinct industries representing five distinct interests. In one part there is the lumber industry. Then we have the national parks. We have the anthracite coal area of Canmore and the subbituminous or soft coal area of Drumheller. We have a mixed farming area north of Calgary and a grain farming area surrounding Drumheller and Munson. One third of the city of Calgary is also in the constituency of Bow River and in the Thornecliffe area are the entrepreneurs and in the Forest Lawn area are the workers. I suggest that it might cost a candidate more to campaign in that constituency than in one where the only industry is farming or coal mining, or a constituency comprised solely of city people.
The second thought I would put forward with regard to setting a specified amount for this purpose, in addition to the fact that constituencies are different, is that today election, campaigns are different from what they used to be. Today we have television which is a very expensive medium, and if one party uses it the other party uses it. What would it cost the country if all election expenses were paid out of the general revenue fund of Canada?
I should like to ask the hon. member this question. How would we control the number of candidates running, for election? In the

constituency of Acadia which adjoins mine I believe that in the last election there were six or seven candidates. We might get 17 or 18 if this idea were adopted. In fact, it might encourage the very thing to which I have always been opposed in this country, the fact that we now have so many splinter parties. This does not only happen on the federal scene but on the provincial scene. The result is that when you look over the records of elections you will find that on most occasions the successful candidate has won with a minority vote simply because it was not a case of a straight vote against the government. I say that if we start to allow a specific sum for anyone who wants to come forward in Canada as a candidate the situation may very well be carried to the extreme and possibly all the 50,000 people in a constituency will want to be candidates. Where do you draw the line?
I said at the beginning that my heart was with the hon. member, but my mind tells me he is wrong. I know what he has in mind. His idea is the same as that in the United States where it is said that any citizen of that country can become president. I still think that in this land of ours anyone who really wishes to become a candidate for a party in an election can do so. When I listen to some people from the far corner of the house I sometimes think that they believe they have a monopoly on the fact that they have come from homes of a kind that do not have too much money to spend on the necessities of life and education. Many of us come from humble surroundings. Irrespective of what party we represent I believe under the free enterprise system in this land of ours any citizen who wishes to become a candidate can become a candidate in an election, be it federal, provincial or at the local level, and get elected. Therefore I do not believe that the system we have today is denying the right to any person to run as a candidate.
In fact, I will go further. The problem is not one of being a candidate but whether you can afford to be a member after you are elected. I think everybody will agree with me on that. Without any animosity toward the socialists I say to them that I believe there is a growing feeling in this country that not only is socialism evident in their own party but it is seeping into industry and is also seeping in the Liberal ranks.
It seems to me that this is another motion placed on the order paper by the socialists because they wish to control elections. They wish to control our elections. There is one country where people have only one candidate to vote for and no doubt in that country the

Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend the hon. member for York South for bringing the motion before the house at this time. The measures he has advocated in his motion are taken for granted in many European countries, as has already been pointed out. There is only one part of his motion that is contentious, but I am prepared to support it in its entirety. First of all, there is the specific proposal relating to expenditures in respect of television, radio and travel incurred by or on behalf of a candidate representing a federal party in a federal election. It is contended these expenses should be paid out of the general revenue. This part of the resolution is contentious, and I should like to let it stand for the moment and proceed with part (b), which reads:
That any additional expenditures by a candidate or by any person or organization on his behalf be limited to a specified amount calculated on the basis of voting population: and (c) that every candidate, constituency organization or federal party and any person or organization acting for or on behalf of any one or all of them shall make full and accurate disclosure of all moneys received and of all expenditures incurred by them in respect of a federal election.
There really is not very much argument left today in respect of these two items. This matter has already been dealt with in England as the mover of the resolution has stated. Back as far as 1888, again in 1918, 1928 and 1948, severe limitations were imposed by the law of the United Kingdom. This measure should have been introduced into Canadian law and would have been long before now except for various circumstances.
For example, the Hon. C. G. Power, a well known Liberal now sitting in the Senate of Canada, was pleading for a limitation on election expenses in 1939.

I will come to that if I have time. It is all right for the hon. member to make these remarks, but I should like to point out that the matter before us is serious indeed. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, I

have a motion similar to the one proposed by the hon. gentleman, but mine goes even a little farther and was incorporated in the Liberal platform in the last election.
I was going to refer to the position taken by the Hon. C. G. Power back in 1939. Ten years later, in 1949, Mr. Power wrote an article in Maclean's magazine. He urged that a ceiling be placed, once and for all, upon the election expenses of candidates. The size of election expenses, he said, brings pressure for putting an end to the stupid and senseless federal election expenses of candidates. As a matter of fact, this measure of reform was introduced by Mr. Power in this parliament in 1938 and reintroduced in the session of 1939. It received extensive study in this house, and in committee, and was reported back to this house with approval and the recommendation that in the next session a bill be introduced. Before that bill could be introduced, the second world war commenced and this matter was pushed aside. It has not been discussed fully since. I think the hon. member must be commended for bringing it up now.
In England, the representation of the people act was passed in 1948 severely limiting the election expenses of candidates. In that connection, I may say that expenses of a candidate in a county constituency were limited to 450 pounds, together with an additional two pence for each entry in the register of parliamentary electors to be used at the election. In a borough constituency another ceiling was placed which made a sharp reduction in election expenses in 1948 as compared with the law of the United Kingdom as it existed before that date. The mother of parliaments, therefore, has taken a stand on this matter which is again before the Canadian House of Commons.
I do believe, Mr. Speaker, it is high time that parliament seriously considered this matter. There have been articles in newspapers and magazines in Canada from year to year on this subject. Mr. Blair Fraser wrote an article in Maclean's magazine-I have not got the year-urging that an end be put to the present system; that it is antiquated. I believe, therefore, it is up to the government to bring forward legislation to limit the expenses. I will not make any further comment on it because I believe such a step is necessary and I will support it. The hon. member is to be commended for bringing this matter forward.
I should like to deal briefly with the part of his motion which states that certain election expenses should be paid for out of the national revenue of Canada. This is a rather contentious matter, I do admit. I gave the

subject some thought, and I was rather surprised when I noticed it in the Liberal platform during the last federal election. I thought, well, if we seriously believe this, then the time has come when this ought to take place. I put a motion on the order paper, therefore, in similar terms to that of the hon. member, and I received a good deal of comment about it. I have discovered this matter should be seriously discussed in parliament before it is brought into effect. I incurred the hostility of my local newspaper when I set my motion on the order paper.
The Brantford Expositor of July 26, 1962 carried a lead editorial entitled, "Paying for Politics." I should like to quote briefly from it:
Like the curate's egg, the proposal of James E. Brown, M.P. for Brantford, that the law relating to parliamentary election expenses should be revised, is good in parts.
The editorial commends the first two parts of my motion which are similar to the hon. member's motion, that is to say, that election expenses should be limited and that the party should be required to give a strict accounting. This editorial was the most definite editorial against my proposal. The newspaper favoured these first two items, and in dealing with the other item the editorial said:
-that the government should pay the legally permitted expenses of any candidate who polls a "reasonable" proportion of the total vote cast, would carry the welfare state idea to a pitch that not even the welfare-minded British have ever thought of.
The government-that is the taxpayer-already foots a $12 million bill for organizing and running the voting machinery. That, no one will doubt, is a proper function of government in a democratic parliamentary system. But to expect every taxpayer to help pick up the tab for every candidate on the ballot, both the one he would like to see elected and those he wouldn't, is carrying things to absurdity.
That is what the Brantford Expositor said at that time. However I was very surprised to find a quotation, in the notes I made on this subject, from the Toronto Globe and Mail of February 9, 1962, which devoted an editorial to the cost of elections and took a divergent view from the Brantford Expositor. It was commenting on the government of Quebec leading the way in Canada to this type of legislation and was more or less praising that government for what it had done in this regard. It said:
The dominion government may be urged to follow the example set by Mr. Lesage, but the matter should be given thorough consideration before being rushed into practice.
It was this very point which prompted me to put something into my motion that is not in the motion of the hon. member for York South. I suggested that this matter be placed 27507-3-128
Canada Elections Act
before the committee on privileges and elections and I would have preferred had the hon. member done that also, because I must admit this is a matter requiring very serious and prolonged discussion. I would like to hear the views of various hon. members, who have considerable experience in the house, on this subject. I wish the hon. member's motion had asked that the matter be referred to that committee, where it would receive more than the one hour's discussion it will receive this evening. The subject is of paramount importance and the time has come to make a great change in Canada's electoral laws.
When the 1948 act was introduced in the British house of commons the home secretary, Mr. Ede, said it was the completion of a long line of reform extending back to the reform bill of 1832, and that the 1948 act was introducing true parliamentary democracy into a modern nation. We must have those reforms in Canada today. I believe these matters will come before the house, despite what is done in tonight's debate, and that in the not too very distant future. I also believe parliament will pass this private legislation and I am certain the hon. member's motion is quite in order at this time and should be considered.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee reported at five o'clock, I was trying to get ahead of the Joneses over here and running into difficulty. But I did want to add one or two other points to the argument, that by extending the hours of sitting we would not speed up the business of the house.
Since the Prime Minister was good enough to give us what has become a rare entry, on his part, into the debate-if it is not impertinent to say so, he did a very fine job in presenting his argument-I thought it was up

to me as a member of this party to express one or two different views. I would turn to the words of the right hon. gentleman himself in order to suggest one of the solutions which is open to him as Prime Minister. I am reading from Hansard of February 1, 1958 where, as reported at page 4200, the right hon. gentleman said:
The present government is supported by 113 members out of a total of 265. Its position as a minority government has become intolerable. No other party or group in this house can possibly form a government: that I want to make clear.
Then there were a number of interruptions, and the Prime Minister went on to say:
At the outset of the present session in October last, assurance was given by the then leader of the opposition that the government might count upon the official opposition not to place obstacles in the way of the government in seeking to carry out the program which was approved by the Canadian electorate on June 10, 1957.
Of course, I point out here that in 1957-58 we had the same co-operative support from the benches of the official opposition. They were willing to go along for a period of time. Then the Prime Minister went on:
The present Leader of the Opposition clearly indicated in his speech in this house on January 20 that the government can no longer expect any continuance of the course announced by his predecessor. Indeed, there have been many statements from opposition sources indicating quite clearly that the government would be defeated in the house as soon as the opposition could contrive it, and that they would welcome a general election.
Then the Prime Minister went on to put on record the reasons for dissolving parliament and having an election. These are the reasons he gave. On January 21, as reported in Hansard on page 3570, when the minister of finance was speaking about lack of courage on the part of the opposition the hon. member for Laurier-the same fellow who was speaking here earlier today- challenged the government by saying: "Bring it on". And the then hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet, now premier of Quebec, said "Hold it". On the previous day, January 20, as reported on page 3524, the Prime Minister said:
When we have the authority we shall do so.
And the hon. member for Laurier said:
Why don't you find out whether or not you have it?
Later on, the Prime Minister said:
Having regard to all the circumstances, the government cannot possibly hope to carry forward its long term program of the development of resources and strengthening of the Canadian economy and the building of a bright future for Canadians unless it can be assured of sufficient support in the house.
So I should like to suggest to the Prime Minister that there is one alternative which

is open to him if he feels he has an obstreperous house and one with which he feels he cannot deal. He has his own words to guide him as spoken on February 1, 1958.
