So I would suggest that the Prime Minister has these two possibilities; he can dissolve parliament or he can respond to that grand suggestion of the Leader of the Opposition and resign and let the Leader of the Opposition take over. These are possibilities which are to be found in the records of their own statements. But I should like to add on behalf of this party a brief comment on one point which the Prime Minister brought up, which was that the western members, or the members from other distant points, tend to carry on the business of parliament while those from nearby do not. I think I agree that this is the case. I am always waiting for the day when some hon. members from the west, such as myself, can go home while the hon. members for Ottawa East and Hochelaga, and Russell, and others like them keep things going. However, I suppose this is really not practical, judging from past experience, and I suggest that members from the west and other distant parts of the country will always carry an inordinate burden until there is a different attitude not on the part of the House of Commons, but taken by the parties as expressed in their discipline.
On another point the Prime Minister made, I should like to suggest that the right hon. gentleman, when he talks about the British example, needs to put forward in much greater detail the advantages the British have with a unitary system of government, a simpler country to run and the kind of procedure which permits many more challenged debates.
This is the factor which I think is the most important one. In the British parliament the press, television and radio give a very skimpy coverage compared with our own country, and the fact is that most members of parliament there really do not speak with one eye on the press gallery or on the lobby for correspondents. The problem in Canada for members of parliament is different, particularly in terms of their own re-election and the role they must play. I have sat in the British house of commons very often, but I have never heard a constituency speech made in that house of the kind we hear here, where hon. members talk of having the constituency which produces the finest apples in Canada, or which has the most beautiful girls in Canada, or about the Kettle Valley railway and things like that.
But seriously, Mr. Chairman, on this particular point, if you are going to put forward the British model, you have to recognize the differences between us. For example, in

Therefore, we feel that this afternoon we had somewhat of an exaggeration of the situation in so far as this house is concerned, and we should like to counsel everyone to have a little patience. Mr. Chairman, I want to come back to earth now. I want to talk about a matter which seriously concerns 200,000 Canadians in southeastern British Columbia. I want to raise a matter on which I have spoken previously in this house, and I do not apologize for speaking on the subject again because I have been asked by various organizations in my constituency to raise this matter at the first opportunity; and this is the first opportunity. The question I wish to speak on is about a continued and improved passenger service on the Kettle valley railway. Before doing so, I want to refer to some remarks made by the hon. member for Laurier when he was chiding the government for not bringing forward legislation. Although the Columbia river treaty is mentioned in the speech from the throne, to date the government has not brought that treaty before the house for ratification. The reason it has not been brought, of course, is that they have no agreement with the government of British Columbia. It has been clearly demonstrated for months that the present government made

a great blunder when our Prime Minister went to Washington to sign that treaty prior to getting agreement with the premier of British Columbia regarding the implementation of the terms of the treaty.
Mr. Chairman, the matter about which I wish to speak is of great concern, and is a question which has been of concern since 1958, when the Canadian Pacific Railway first gave consideration to a reduction of passenger services. This passenger service in question was reduced from a standard train service between Hope, in British Columbia, and Medicine Hat, in Alberta, to a Budd car with no sleeping accommodation and no restaurant accommodation. At that time there was a general protest from all types of organizations in the constituency-chambers of commerce, trade unions, farmers organizations, municipalities. Various churches protested, and other groups of representatives in the area served between Hope and the Alberta-British Columbia border also protested. But regardless of those protests, the C.P.R. reduced this service at that time.
To indicate the concern, I just want to quote very briefly from the Nelson daily News of February 13, 1959. The headline is: "End to 'deplorable rail service' demanded by Nelson chamber. Public urged to tell of inconveniences suffered". The article goes on:
Nelson chamber of commerce wired transport minister Hon. George Hees and attorney general Robert Bonner Thursday requesting that immediate consideration be given the "deplorable rail service provided this area at the present time/'
Then on March 3, 1960, the Nelson daily News again carried the headline: "Attorney general seeks Kootenay train service". In a report datelined Victoria, the following appeared:
Attorney general Bonner intends to take up again with the chairman of the board of transport commissioners the question of renewal of full-time train service through the Doukhobor areas of the Kootenays, he told the legislature Wednesday night.
The minister replied to Kootenay member questioners in the house that the province had offered to pay a third of the cost up to $50,000 of railway protection through the Doukhobor area, providing the federal government and the C.P.R. absorbed the other two thirds.
The board of transport commissioners had promised to make an order compelling the C.P.R. to restore full service "if we would guarantee the safety of the trains."
The "we" that is the government of British Columbia.
After having suffered that reduced passenger service since 1959 the C.P.R. has made application to the board of transport commissioners to abandon passenger service on the Kettle Valley railway, a service which serves, as I mentioned before, a population of nearly 200,000 people in south eastern British

Columbia, one of the richest producing areas in the province where there is up to nearly $270 million worth production from the mines and forests of the area, and from the fruit growing lands and farming districts. This reduction in service has caused a great deal of resentment throughout the area. I have in my hand the Nelson daily News for July 25, 1962, which carries the headline: "Natal brief to detail reasons for passenger service deficit". The reason that the C.P.R. give for discontinuing this passenger service is lack of patronage. Naturally there is a lack of patronage when we are reduced to a Budd car and a split service at Penticton where people coming from Vancouver to Nelson, for instance, have to lie over at night in Penticton and carry on their journey the next day. That causes people to use buses and other forms of transportation. This point is mentioned in the article. The report says:
Natal village commission has gone on record as opposing an application by the Canadian Pacific Railway to the board of transport commissioners to discontinue passenger service between Lethbridge and Spence's Bridge.
The village will notify the railway company and the board of its intention to file a protest brief. Purpose of the brief is to point out some of the obvious reasons for the large deficit suffered in the operations.
In referring to the company's statement that an average of only 15 persons used the service daily between any given points on the line, chairman Orlando Ungaro said he was not at all surprised. He said the travelling public could not be blamed for failing to patronize the kind of service given.
That short comment in the press is similar to the comment f recieved from numerous organizations in my constituency and other constituencies with respect to the present service and the reason for its not being patronized to a much greater extent. I think I can make my remarks as brief as possible by simply quoting from a editorial in the Nelson daily News. I am not accustomed to quoting this paper frequently as it is a strong supporter of the present government and extremely critical of the hon. member for Kootenay West a great deal of the time. However, in this instance it represents the opinion of the people in the area. As this is the opinion of their subscribers, of course, they realize that this represents a large body of public opinion with respect to this question. The editorial is entitled "Rail passenger service still a necessity" and it reads as follows:
Once again, the chambers of commerce and municipal and other interested bodies are faced with the task of attempting to save the southern section of the interior of B.C. from losing a public transportation service.
It is the second time within five years that train passenger service to the area has become a matter of concern for these groups. In the interim few have given the railway's passenger service much
Interim Supply
more than passing thought except during those periods when travellers have been unable to use the air services or felt road conditions made car or bus travel unpleasant.
I might mention the fact that we are particularly dependent upon rail traffic in the southeastern part of British Columbia in certain periods of the winter. For instance, planes are not allowed to land at Castlegar airport if the clouds are below the mountain tops, and that condition occurs quite frequently during the winter months. Also bus traffic can become very uncertain during heavy snowfall conditions when buses are tied up because of deep snow and snow plowing at certain high elevations. The editorial continues:
Those periods are quite frequent in the winter months and it is for this reason that the public bodies now are willing to fight to retain a passenger service on the rails.
It is time that the general opinion is stated that the rail diesel car operation cannot be termed a good service as it has been operated.
Had the C.P.R. given a better service, which means a faster, cleaner, non-stop service with provision for meals, the situation would now be different. If the railway had promoted the service the situation would now be different. If the granting of the franchise had not carried with it concessions in land and natural resources the situation would have been different.
It would have been different because a better attempt to provide a good service and a normal attempt to promote that service would have left the opponents on thin ice.
It is not usual for chambers of commerce in particular to take the position that they should dispute the right of private business to regulate its own affairs but in this instance, where there has been a granting of concessions, most believe there is an undertaking to provide not only a freight but also a passenger service.
It would be unreasonable to expect the railway company to operate the Kootenay division at a loss in perpetuity. It seems highly likely that freight will in future pay the bills, so that we in the Kootenay must accept the dropping of the passenger service in time, provided a good, reliable alternate service is available.
In the meantime, we in the Kootenay must demand a continued rail passenger service and/or proof that a good service well promoted would not come closer to paying its way.
I might say that, at the same time consideration is being given to the dropping of the passenger service on the Kettle valley railway, consideration is also being given to lessening bus service from the Alberta border to Vancouver. Hence we are faced with this twin possibility of lack of adequate passenger service.
The government of Canada gave the Canadian Pacific Railway millions of acres of land and billions of dollars worth of natural resources in exchange for the building of a railroad that applies to all Canada. It seems that the C.P.R. has now forgotten all about these fabulous grants it received for providing services to the public. The C.P.R. continues

Interim Supply
to enjoy and profit from full possession of land and resources granted long ago but insists that all present services must be directly related to present profits derived from these services. Hardly a week goes by without the C.P.R. doing its best to dispose of an agent, as happened in southeastern British Columbia and on the prairies, or to discontinue passenger service or abandon a branch line. This principle or this practice is not only complained of by people in southeastern British Columbia but it is going on all over western Canada.
The current proposal of the C.P.R. to abandon passenger service on the Kettle valley railway will be vehemently opposed by organizations in general and by the people. It is bad enough already that the C.P.R., which is the major stockholder in the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, should operate the Kettle valley line basically for the convenience of its subsidiary and not to the advantage of the public and of the industrial workers in that area. In our opinion the board of transport commissioners should refuse to authorize any further removal of agents, curtailment of services or abandonment of branch lines until a complete and co-ordinated national transportation policy has been worked out. In the opinion of members of this group this alone can ensure efficiency for the railways, justice for their workers, convenience for our people and progress for our Canadian communities affected.
In this instance I suggest a somewhat different procedure than the one which is being followed at the present time by the application to the board of transport commissioners by the C.P.R. to abandon passenger service on that railway. I urge the Minister of Transport to use his good offices to get a senior official of the C.P.R. to go to the district. If he will do that, I am sure the various representative organizations in the district will make arrangements for a meeting of representatives of the municipalities, trade unions -and this matter affects all the trade unionists in the area-all chambers of commerce, women's institutes, farmers' institutes and numerous other community organizations to meet with the senior official of the C.P.R. Let the senior official of the C.P.R. tell these people what the company's needs are. We want both sides of the question aired. We want to be fair about this thing. Let the people of the district inform the senior official of their problems. Then as a result of learning of the company's position and the company learning of the needs of the people I trust there can be built up a co-operation between the company and the people of the

area that will make it possible for this railroad to be patronized to a greater extent and operated to the advantage of the people and without loss to the company.

I was greatly interested in the follow-up that was made this afternoon by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to certain questions I raised as to the legality of some $200 million in a year of tariff taxation imposed by the executive by order in council on June 24 and which I raised at the time we were considering Bill No. C-81, to amend the Customs Tariff. I then said that I could not under any conceivable reading of the basic statute believe that any lawyer or any layman in this House of Commons, if he read section 22 of the Financial Administration Act, could imagine that anybody could found upon that section a determination to abate customs duties imposed in another statute, as I knew that it would involve hundreds of thousands of transactions through the customs entry points of this country. I think the Minister of Finance was sensitive to my criticism last week because hon. members will recall that he rose and said that I must have some kind of pipe line to his officials to get information that would give me this impression that in a practical way it would not be possible to administer the order in council of June 24 last. I, of course, challenged his statement and said that I was informed by those outside government concerned with customs entries throughout the country when I said that it was very unlikely that records were being kept.
Like the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, I say that you cannot have it both ways. You cannot say that section 22 of the Financial Administration Act is big enough and wide enough in scope to enable the cabinet to found thereon the order in council of June 24 last and respect it in one part and then come, as the government has come today, and say that they cannot adhere to it in so far as the stipulation in subsection 8 of section 22 is concerned, which states that any remission of customs duty beyond the value of $1,000 must be reported to this parliament.
The ministry says this afternoon, in answering question 900 on the order paper, that they have not respected that section of the statute. They say, indeed, that it is not a practical working section that can be administered. That was the basis of my criticism last week. I say it was not contemplated when this particular provision was enacted

that it would be used other than in exceptional circumstances. However on June 24th this administration chose to use it as a broad gate for the imposition in an indirect way of $200 million in customs tariff taxation, which action they do not up to now propose to bring before parliament for ratification.
We had a great deal of discussion this afternoon about the efficient use of the time of the house. We have had several opportunities to refer to this particular June order in council. I say that if the administration were not sensitive of their weakness in using and abusing this statute we would have had this order in council brought before parliament for ratification in the same way that in 1947 the former administration came to parliament after an exchange crisis developed and at the first possible opportunity to have parliament ratify what the executive had done.
We heard the Prime Minister this afternoon, following the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He began by saying, good, pugnacious lawyer that he is, and significantly to some of us, "I do not intend to deal with the legality of the matter raised by the member for Winnipeg North Centre". He said, "1 prefer the opinion of the law officers of the crown". Then he went on to something quite different from the challenge of great importance advanced by the member for Winnipeg North Centre. I simply want to say that this is not characteristic of the Prime Minister, with his legal ability and his argumentative talents, to pass off in that way the very important challenge that was raised this afternoon. In addition, when there is talk in this house about wasting time in getting down to essentials, members of the committee must recall that the opinion advanced by the law officers of the crown has been sought in this house through a motion moved by my deskmate, the hon. member for Essex East. In rising to speak on this item, I make no apologies for taking up a few minutes of the time of the committee because this is the first time I have spoken this session. I do want to take this opportunity of referring to a matter that I might call a grievance, although actually I do not want to use that term. I would rather say that I hope to be able to add my voice to the other voices in challenging Canadian industry to wake up from its deep sleep and recognize that Canada is no longer in a seller's market. We are in a buyer's market. If we want to maintain our trade, if we want to expand our export trade, it is just useless to sit in offices and hope that trade is going to come to us or that somehow or other the government is going to be able to place it in our laps.

Some three years ago I said that I thought we were not awake in Canada as we should be in view of changing world conditions. I am more than ever convinced that something has got to be done to get a great many of manufacturing and export industries of Canada to realize they have to go out and fight to expand our trade. It has got to be brought home to manufacturers in Canada that they have a responsibility to take advantage of the paths that are made available by the government for them to reach the new markets outside of Canada.
It was my privilege, just over a week ago, to attend the international trade fair that was held in the capital city of Lagos. I fully realize that the Canadian government put on a prestige fair in west Africa all by themselves, and that was all to the good. We have just finished participating in a three week trade fair in west Africa where the Canadian government, through the Department of Trade and Commerce, made a pavilion available to Canadian industrialists and manufacturers. We Canadians visiting Lagos went to see that pavilion and we were disappointed. We felt frustrated and disgusted with the reaction of Canadian industry in failing to take advantage of that pavilion and trying to add to our home employment and better our economy by endeavouring to obtain the new markets available in west Africa.
I shall detain the committee just a few minutes to describe the pavilion. First of all it must be made known that the Department of Trade and Commerce offered space in the pavilion free of charge to any manufacturer interested. The Canadian government also paid for the freight transport of all the goods on display. What was the result? You went into one display booth, operated by or on behalf of one of the biggest manufacturing corporations in Canada, a corporation that manufactures farm implements, pumps, refrigerators, deep freezers, washing machines and all kinds of machinery. It was a display booth about eight feet by three feet six and the main item on display was one small water pump.
There was no Canadian there to explain what it was all about, and the company paid $85 to a west African student to look after the display stall. During the three weeks of the fair three-quarters of a million Nigerians attended it, made up of thousands of teenagers, students, the mass of the population, the members of the legislature, the premiers, the lieutenant governor and all the administrators.
When I was there the governor of eastern Nigeria and his head administrators showed keen interest in the water pump and said 27507-3-129
Interim Supply
they could use thousands of them in Nigeria. He asked how it worked, but the poor African student didn't know. He tried to explain but he got it all backwards. The governor then asked what it worked on and the answer was petrol. He asked could it be used with an electric motor and the student replied he did not know. He asked if it was the type of pump that could be submerged in a well and again the answer was that the student did not know. He asked was it the type of pump that could be used in a creek, and again the answer by the student was that he did not know. I repeat that this was the booth of one of the biggest corporations in Canada, which had its equipment sent over free and its display space provided free. That is how it is trying to get into the export business.
There was also a three-display section of refrigerators and deep freezers. They were good displays but there was no Canadian there to explain them. The governor of Nigeria was interested in them. He said "This is what we need". He opened every drawer and pulled out every tray and asked to whom they could go in Nigeria to inquire about this equipment. The answer was that there was nobody. The company had no agents in west Africa to display Canadian equipment and nobody to explain it.
I just want to mention one more incident in order to get this point across. Nigeria, in the northern region, is a land of forests, where they cut down their trees with machetes. Mr. Chairman, you ought to see them. At the back of the hotel where we stayed in Lagos the manager wanted to have a tree cut down. I measured it and it had a 10 inch butt. It took a man a day and a half to cut the tree with a machete and it needed five men with a rope to pull it down the way they wanted it to fall. With a power saw it could have been down in five minutes. Oh yes, a Canadian manufacturer had a power saw on display. There was the African student who was paid $85 to look after the display, and the power saw display consisted of one saw on a shelf.
I was surrounded by teenage students who asked me what it was. I said it was a power saw. They asked what use did it have, but that is something which is pretty hard to explain. They asked was there any literature to describe it, and I found out the literature had run out during the first week. If we wanted to sell power saws the way to do it was to have a log in front of the stall and, every half hour or so, use the saw on it to show how efficiently it could operate.
The whole affair was just not good enough, and somehow or other we have got to make

Interim Supply
our manufacturers understand that they have a responsibility to themselves and to the people of Canada. Other countries are certainly going to beat us in the export field, and I can give an example of this. We went through all the pavilions in the fair, and the manufacturers of all the other countries were on the job, trying to sell their products and get into this vast potential market in Africa.
Right next door to the Canadian pavilion was the Russian pavilion. We may sneer at communism and we do not like it, but they were out to sell their goods and to sell their principles at the same time. It was a real eye-opener to go through the Russian pavilion. The first thing that struck the visitor was their propaganda, and they showed their psychological understanding of that right down to the nth degree. The first thing you see is a sign reading "Peace", and at the end of the booth is a great big sign reading "Peace, liberty, freedom, equality, fraternity, happiness." The wall is just as wide as this chamber and about half as high, and in great big lettering it carries "What communism means to you. By 1980 free education, free health services, complete maintenance of children, rent free housing, free midday meals, free holiday resorts, grants to unmarried mothers" -and that means a lot in that country.
In between the psychological propaganda is the equipment they want to sell, and they use the good psychology of not showing it on the floor. It is raised up on platforms so that no matter how many hundreds or thousands of people there may be in the pavilion they can all see the machinery. The machinery is working and is being demonstrated, and instead of one lone black student they had quite a few black students together with 85 English speaking Russians to demonstrate, explain and hand out literature by the thousands of pieces.
I wish to mention one other item with regard to the Canadian pavilion which skipped my mind a moment ago. There was one company which had a display there and which had somebody from Canada in charge of it. It was an Ontario company which was trying to introduce cheese into the African market. It had a good display of cheese, and cheese that was a credit to Canada. The Africans, not knowing about cheese, had to taste it. However, in order to taste it they had to pay a shilling a slice. When one thinks of the millions upon millions of pounds of butter and cheese which we are storing in Canada, he must contrast that with this effort to charge a shilling for cheese at a trade fair in west Africa. I did want to raise this question because, unless we are complete fools and completely blind we must realize we are in a

buyers' market; we must realize that the expansion of Canada and full employment in Canada depend on our maintenance and expansion of foreign trade. This demands that we do a selling job where markets are open. I say it is a disgrace and a betrayal, the fact that so many of our Canadian industries and manufacturers are not doing anything to help themselves. I believe we owe it to the country as members of parliament to tell them that any and all governments will do everything possible to assist them in the expansion of their foreign trade, but they have to do something to help themselves.
Each and every one of us should be interested in this subject because we know there is unemployment; we want to help the unemployed to get work. In our society as it is today, the ordinary way for a man or woman to go to work is to get a job in industry. In order to provide such jobs under our present system, the industry concerned has to make a profit, so we have to tell them: Go out and do something for yourselves; get out and sell; do a two fold job which is not being done now-sell the principles of democracy and sell quality Canadian goods.

It seems to me we should have some understanding from the government that a committee to deal with defence expenditures will be set up. I would point out to this committee of the whole that out of the controllable expenditure as distinct from the statutory expenditure, over one and a half billion dollars out of three and a billion dollars, or nearly one half, is spent on defence. In other words, nearly one half of the controllable expenditure of the taxpayer's dollar goes into defence.
There is a tremendous possibility of waste in this field of defence and research, if for no other reason than the rapid changes of technology which lead to immense sums being spent on obsolete equipment. I will take an example, not from Canada but from Britain where it is now acknowledged one hundred million pounds sterling, or approximately $300 million was spent on developing the Blue Streak rocket which became obsolete before it was even ready for testing. I appreciate that this question of defence is linked up with policy, which latter consideration is the prerogative of the government. However, I believe that a defence committee could bring together a group of people in this house including, for example, such persons as the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount and others who have gained experience in this field and may be able to serve one of the essential functions of the

Interim Supply
house, which is to scrutinize the tremendous expenditures which are inevitable today on defence. They would be able to contribute something, not only to the question of security which arises out of this, but also to a most important matter affecting our pocket-books.
I noticed that the other day, in answering a question from the Leader of the Opposition, the Prime Minister said that the government would make known its decision in this regard very shortly. I suggest that before we go too far into the work of the house in this particular session we should hear from the government whether it proposes to set up a committee. The Prime Minister spoke today very eloquently about the need for the effective functioning of parliament. It seems to me that this parliament cannot very well function effectively, Mr. Chairman, when nearly one-half or one-third of our expenditures are not subject to any effective scrutiny by the members of this house.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to support the proposal put forward by the hon. member for Greenwood, that the government ought to ask the house to establish a committee to look into the question of defence expenditures, because so far parliament has found itself in great difficulty in obtaining the information it needs to consider the government's defence policy and government expenditures in relation to its defence policy- if it has one, as some of us find difficult to believe at times.
I put a question on the order paper last month directed to the minister of defence, asking if he had been advised whether a Bo-marc armed with a nuclear warhead would neutralize an atomic or thermo-nuclear device if it were to come into contact with it in the air. The minister replied to that question on October 29 and said that responsible scientific and military authorities had given the ministry to understand that there was a high probability-that was the expression the minister used-that a Bomarc armed with a nuclear warhead would in fact neutralize an atomic or thermo-nuclear device being carried by an aircraft or a missile, on contact therewith. Of course, as members of the house will recall, this was a disclosure which had previously been made by the minister of defence in a letter which he wrote to Maclean's magazine some time ago.
It was interesting that the answer given to the house by the minister was qualified, in that he was able to tell us, not that it had been confirmed that a Bomarc armed with a nuclear warhead would neutralize an atomic or thermo-nuclear device upon contact, but simply that the government had been advised
[Mr. Brewin.l
that such was a high probability. Therefore a further question was placed on the order paper seeking to find out if the advice the ministry had received had been qualified in any way, whether any actual tests had been conducted to determine that in fact a Bomarc would neutralize an atomic or thermo-nuclear device on contact, and also seeking to ascertain whether the government had been advised that any device had been perfected or means had been found of avoiding the neutralization of an atomic or thermo-nuclear device in those circumstances.
The minister answered that question on November 21 by, in effect, declining to give any further information, saying that the information upon which the official Canadian view was based had been obtained from other countries and was subject to the security classification placed upon it by those other countries. Then the minister said, as reported on page 1857 of Hansard:
Specific answers to the further questions posed by the hon. member cannot be provided without revealing information which is highly classified, and would obviously be of assistance to any potential enemy.
So that we have this peculiar situation. The minister had made a disclosure about the effect of a missile armed with a nuclear warhead upon contact with a nuclear weapons carrier, and then had left us in suspense when the question had been further developed on the order paper, and resorted to the argument that this information was classified and that to provide any further information would be of assistance to a potential enemy.
I fail to see how the minister could disclose in a national publication certain information, and then decline to disclose certain related information to the House of Commons itself. I fail to understand the minister's argument in that respect, but this at any rate illustrates why this house requires a committee on defence expenditures to get to the root of this matter. If the house were able to establish a committee to look into this and other matters which would naturally arise from a consideration of defence expenditures, the house would not be handicapped and neither would the government. Such a committee might, if it became necessary, hold in camera hearings, with appropriate witnesses, to determine whether the information which the minister saw fit to give to the house was correct, whether the information which the minister saw fit not to give the house was in fact correct, and whether that latter information ought really to have been divulged to the house when the matter was raised on the order paper.

For these reasons, Mr. Chairman, I urge the government to give most serious consideration to the suggestion put forward by the hon. member for Greenwood. I suggest that the minister of defence was not justified in disclosing certain information which related to this most important question, in disclosing information relating to the so-called probability of a missile armed with a nuclear warhead neutralizing an atomic or thermonuclear device upon contact, and then at a later stage, when the questions were getting very close to the heart of a matter of the gravest concern to the people of this country -because military considerations enter into the question whether Canada should acquire nuclear weapons-see fit to hide behind the argument that the information was classified and that it would be of assistance to a potential enemy. Mr. Chairman, I do not think the minister was justified in resorting to this argument; but if he was, the only way to deal with the matter is to refer it to a committee on defence expenditures, and for that reason I support the extremely useful suggestion that has been put forward by the hon. member for Greenwood.

The information requested is not available as detailed statistics are not maintained pertaining to the application of the surcharge on imports order.
It is one thing to say to me as the member asking the question today that the information the member wants is not available today, but what this answer says is that the detailed information necessary to comply with the requirements of the Financial Administration Act a year or two from now is not being maintained, and the answer in that sentence admits quite openly that the information which is not being maintained is that which pertains to the application of the surcharge on imports order.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that that means that the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue and those responsible for administering this have read the surcharge on imports order and have read section 22, subsection 8, of the Financial Administration Act and they know what is called for; but they say quite frankly that the information pertaining to the application of the surcharge on imports order is not being maintained. I can see what will happen a couple of years from now when the public accounts for this year come out and the information is not there. Someone will get up and ask why it is not there and the answer will have to be, by whatever minister is in charge at that time, that the information was not maintained back in 1962 as required by the Financial Administration Act.
As the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River says, this is not fun and games and the minister cannot slough this off by the old appeal to get the interim supply bill through so that civil service salaries will be paid. Do not worry about that. Pay day is a few days off yet.

speechtext:
Still frozen civil service
salaries.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT REQUIRING DISCLOSURE OF CAMPAIGN FUND CONTRIBUTIONS
speechtext:
Yes, that is another speech I intended to make, but time is getting on.
Let me get back to this. The minister cannot slough off the seriousness of this issue by reference to fun and games or by appeals to get the bill through. The plain and simple matter is that we have been told today on the authority of a responsible minister of the crown, the Minister of National Revenue, that the detailed statistics are not being maintained pertaining to the application of the surcharge on imports order. Now, that says just as clearly as Mr. Garson did in 1949 that he had not carried out the provisions of the law for the reasons which were good enough to him, that this government is not carrying out the provisions of section 22, subsection 8 of the Financial Administration Act for reasons that this government thinks are satisfactory.
I could digress, Mr. Chairman, and put this question to the Minister of Finance. Is it not beginning to dawn on him that the advice the government got that it had authority to pass this order in council must have been rather flimsy advice? Now, as the government tries to carry out the provisions of that order in council that it passed on the basis of these two statutes, it has got itself into this difficult situation. As I said this afternoon, the excuse given is that during the period my question covers, from June 24 to October 31, 1962, there were 2,205,236 import entries. In other words the task of carrying out the law has become an impossibility, according to the government.
I suggest to the minister it is clear that the Financial Administration Act, section 22, was never intended as a means for raising taxes. The very difficulty we have now shows that any lawyer, I do not care what his title may be, who advised the government it had authority to do this was not giving sound advice whatever. The whole of this action by the government is brought into focus, as I say, by this answer that came down today. I still remember June 24 when the Prime Minister said this would all be brought before parliament. We are still waiting for the order itself. In the meantime, with this answer, we have the same kind of thing that Mr. Garson gave us in 1949 when he explained that he had not carried out the law of that day. I remind the

Minister of Finance and others of the Progressive Conservative party who were here in those days what we thought of that action. Here is the same thing, the executive failing to carry out the clear wording of the law.
I suggest that when the Minister of Finance stands up and tells me this is fun and games or we should get the bill through so that civil servants can get their frozen salaries, that is not good enough in this high court of parliament where, if anything matters, it is respect for the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT REQUIRING DISCLOSURE OF CAMPAIGN FUND CONTRIBUTIONS
speechtext:
No one has said anything about frozen civil servants' salaries. I did suggest it was very important to get this resolution through for reasons which are well known to all responsible members of the House of Commons. I would say, too, that if fun and games was ever justified-perhaps it is not-in describing the actions and antics of an hon. member, it would be when the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre apparently came into the House of Commons this afternoon with a piece of paper. No one had seen it before. He says it was filed by the Minister of National Revenue. It does not appear in Hansard. No one has a record of it. We have only his word for it, plus the fact that apparently the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River was able to get a glance at it.
We have been hearing now for two hours an argument based on this answer which members of the House of Commons have not had an opportunity of seeing. When you read the question you find it refers to a period from June 24, 1962 to October 31, 1962 and asks how many remissions of customs duties were made under the provisions of section 2 of the surcharge on imports order, P.C. 1962902, as based on section 22 of the Financial Administration Act. This is rather a complicated question.

speechtext: Not if you read it.

speechtext: We have had a two hour debate on something-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT REQUIRING DISCLOSURE OF CAMPAIGN FUND CONTRIBUTIONS
speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman. The Minister of Finance says he is not questioning my word.
Interim Supply
I should like to know what else he did. When he rose he said that I came into the house with a piece of paper. The sheet of paper that I have I did not have when I came into the house this afternoon. It was delivered to me 15 or 20 minutes after my question No. 900 had been called from the chair; the Minister of National Revenue had said, "Answered"; the Speaker had repeated "Answered", and the minister had handed to Hansard the original copy of the answer to my question. A copy was delivered to me, and it has initials on it which I recognize. If there is any suggestion that what I have in my possession is not what is on the pages of Hansard today, then the matter of my question will be the subject of a motion to refer the whole question to the committee on privileges and elections.
My good friend the Minister of Finance says he is not doubting my possession of the correct answer, but that is certainly what he has done. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that I know the rules about not having the right to quote in this house something that has been said in a debate until the official copy of Hansard has come down. This was not something that was said. These words were not spoken. This was an official document handed in and a copy of it was given to me as a matter of courtesy because I was the person who had asked the question. Any suggestion that the minister now makes that I should console myself in patience and wait until tomorrow to see if this is the answer that is in Hansard, is not valid. I will certainly be looking at that rather carefully the first thing tomorrow morning to make sure Hansard shows the answer that was in this document that was sent to me. There is, as I say, on the document, a set of initials that I happen to recognize but since they are those of a senior civil servant I will not mention them.
Perhaps I have extended my question of privilege too long. I am sure the Minister of Finance did not mean what he said, and I ask him to withdraw any suggestion I have broken any rule or custom in raising this matter. I suggest I have brought before this house what is an official answer of the Minister of National Revenue. He has to deal with that answer, and he does not do so by the kind of reflection he has just made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT REQUIRING DISCLOSURE OF CAMPAIGN FUND CONTRIBUTIONS
speechtext:
I made no reflection whatever. I say again it is a very strange procedure when we have a two hour debate based on an answer handed to the hon. member and of which other members of the house and the house itself is not seized and will not be until tomorrow.

Interim Supply
There has been some imputation here that there must be something wrong; that there is something to be covered up. What is the date of this question asked by my hon. friend? Sometimes when I heard him labouring tonight I thought we were back in 1956. The question is dated November 22, four days ago.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT REQUIRING DISCLOSURE OF CAMPAIGN FUND CONTRIBUTIONS
speechtext: Did you see it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT REQUIRING DISCLOSURE OF CAMPAIGN FUND CONTRIBUTIONS
speechtext: No, I did not. The question was dated November 22, and if there was any allegation of anything that had to be covered up, anything which should not have been produced, it would have been the easiest thing in the world not to answer it. We have to deal with one facet of this, and if we had examined-how many entries?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT REQUIRING DISCLOSURE OF CAMPAIGN FUND CONTRIBUTIONS
speechtext: Two million.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT REQUIRING DISCLOSURE OF CAMPAIGN FUND CONTRIBUTIONS
speechtext:
-two million, we could have answered this question by saying we are studying the matter, studying these two million entries, for a year and a half. We would never have had to produce anything because we could always have been working on it.
It was answered so quickly and brought in, I think 20 minutes after the hon. member said he stood up to speak, that that is about as good an answer as can be given to the allegation that something is wrong with the situation. This was one question that, if we had wanted to delay answering, I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will agree we could have delayed answering it for a very long time and no one could have objected.
The fact that there happened to be two million entries does not mean that the provisions of the Financial Administration Act are not being properly kept, and I suggest to my hon. friends opposite and to my hon. friends in the lower corner, especially to those who have had experience in administration of government that no one can believe for one minute that the government can make out payments of $1,000 and not have a record kept of them. It may not have a record under the peculiar-I shall not say peculiar but special-wording of this subsection, dealing with the question my hon. friend has raised; but I can assure my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre, and the house and the country, that when the government of Canada, whether it be this government or its predecessors, and I hope any other government, pays out money, whether it is $1,000 or not, a record is kept of it.
I know I had to get an order in council on one occasion when one of my income tax collectors had the seat of his pants tom out by a bulldog. I had to get an order in council to pay $15, but that appeared in the public accounts, and our accounting is so detailed

that no one need have any worry whatsoever about our accounts not being properly kept or that due notice will not be given under the proper circumstances.
It may be understood that in asking the question which the hon. member asked on November 24, and with the answer which came down quite quickly from the civil servants who are so efficient and expert, that he may have had an answer which superficially looks as if some records are not being kept. But I can assure the committee that the records are being kept, and if the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will give us time to produce them, they will be produced at the proper time in the public accounts next spring. If he wants them earlier I think that can be done, although I do not want to give a guarantee on that at the moment; but I do not want any imputation or any suggestion that the proper records are not being kept of every cent and every dollar that is being paid out by this government, whether it is in surcharges or whatever it may be.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT REQUIRING DISCLOSURE OF CAMPAIGN FUND CONTRIBUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance says that he is still convinced that in due time, and dear knows under what administration and with what inconvenience to civil servants, that it will be possible to give to parliament, as is required under the statute, a report of every remission over $1,000 as required under the June 24, 1962, order in council. I say I do not believe it. I have seen copies of the customs entries, and in them there is simply a reference to the net tariff applicable after recognition of all that was done by this fanciful order in council. That is why the minister said to me last week that I must have talked with those who deal with these things and must have a pipe line to convince me that it would not be practical to adhere to the provisions under section 22 of the Financial Administration Act.
In so far as answers to questions are concerned, they are the responsibility of the ministry. The minister tried to pass that off on to civil servants tonight, and I think that was rather unfair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT REQUIRING DISCLOSURE OF CAMPAIGN FUND CONTRIBUTIONS
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT REQUIRING DISCLOSURE OF CAMPAIGN FUND CONTRIBUTIONS
speechtext:
Yes he did. If you read your Hansard you will find he said that in the last three or four days perhaps some civil servants provided this answer to parliament. Parliament asks questions of the ministry and the ministry is responsible for the answers and they cannot pass off that responsibility.
As a matter of fact, with this debate coming up, I was surprised that we would get this naive answer; but we did get it and it

is in conformity with the expectation I raised in debate last week when I said that this act could not possibly be stretched for the purposes of the June 24 order in council by the cabinet because I envisaged that it would involve recognition of these hundreds of thousands of customs entries and an equally binding obligation under the same section of the act to give to parliament, in the public accounts, a report of anything that involved a remission of $1,000 or more of duty.
That is the issue. In June, during the emergency, the government wanted to impose customs surcharges ranging from 5 per cent to 15 per cent on hundreds of items in our customs tariif, and from some source which they will not divulge to parliament, the government obtained some fancy legal opinion that section 22 of the Financial Administration Act could be stretched for this purpose. It cannot be stretched one way if it is not to be used in the other way to report to parliament as parliament has asked.
Everyone in the house knows why there was a necessity to report to parliament. The point was that under the first part of section 22 the governor in council, which is the cabinet, was given the authority on recommendation of the treasury board to remit a tax that would otherwise be legally payable. Now, no one in the house would want the cabinet to have that permission without limit, so parliament put a limit upon it and said it did not want political favours to be given by
Business of the House
tax remission, and it limited this executive action to cases where the treasury board felt that something that parliament had basically established as a tax should be remitted because of special circumstances, and when that was done it should be reported to parliament in the public accounts if the value was over $1,000.
These things are not now being reported. I do not think they can be reported in public accounts despite the assurance of the minister.
We are not going to conclude this debate tonight. I want the minister tomorrow, or when we continue this debate, to present us with some examples from the customs entry forms which will establish and demonstrate that it would be possible for the administration to go back on those 2,205,235 import entries that have passed through 276 ports of entry since the executive decided to impose $200 million of taxation by executive order in council.
Progress reported.
